strengths: Addresses an interesting and practically relevant problem: zero-shot, single-forward-pass 3D stylization from unposed multi-view inputs, removing per-scene optimization required by prior 3DGS/NeRF stylization methods.

The proposed voxel-based 3D style loss is a sensible extension of AdaIN-style statistics matching into 3D space, and the progressive formulation (image-level -> scene-level -> 3D voxel-level) is clearly presented.

Clean architectural design that disentangles geometry (self-attention backbone path, VGGT-initialized) from style (global cross-attention conditioning), preserving geometric fidelity while transferring appearance.

Includes ablations on style-content coupling strategies and style losses with reasonable consistency metrics (short/long-range LPIPS/RMSE, ArtScore), and demonstrates cross-category (CO3D) and cross-scene (DL3DV -> Tanks and Temples) generalization.
Appendix provides loss pseudo-code and efficiency/memory scaling analysis, supporting reproducibility efforts.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparison: only StyleRF and StyleGS, both per-scene optimization methods, making the comparison setup somewhat apples-to-oranges (zero-shot feed-forward model vs. per-scene tuned weights). The closest concurrent method, Styl3R, is not compared; the paper's claim of state-of-the-art rests on a narrow benchmark of four Tanks and Temples scenes.

Novelty is incremental: the geometry backbone, camera/depth heads, voxelization, and Gaussian adapter are directly inherited from VGGT and AnySplat; the main new components are the cross-attention style aggregator and the 3D style loss, both of which are relatively small modifications of known techniques (AdaIN/cross-attention conditioning).

Quantitative gains are modest and somewhat inconsistent: the 3D style loss improves long-range LPIPS only marginally (0.147 -> 0.140) and the scene loss actually degrades short-range metrics; no statistical significance or variance reporting, and no user study to substantiate the stylization quality claims.

Qualitative results show fairly weak/conservative stylization in many appendix figures (several scenes are barely distinguishable from unstyled content), which weakens the central claim of 'high-quality zero-shot stylization'; the method also degrades notably beyond 32 views per batch, contradicting the claimed scalability to 'hundreds of views'.

No evaluation of reconstruction/geometry quality against feed-forward reconstruction baselines (e.g., AnySplat, VGGT) to verify that the framework does not sacrifice geometric fidelity, and ArtScore evaluation details for baselines are not described.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission: code not released (promised upon acceptance), and key hyperparameters (loss weights, voxel grid resolution, training schedule details) are not reported in the main text.

Presentation issues: duplicated Tanks and Temples citations, typos (e.g., 'imamge', 'discontinues'), incomplete sentence in the abstract ('Our codes will be available at'), and missing implementation details for resolution and training scale.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: single-forward, zero-shot 3D stylization without per-scene optimization or precomputed poses, which is a practically meaningful setting.

The architecture is clearly described, and the disentanglement of geometry (self-attention backbone path) and style (global cross-attention conditioning) is a reasonable design choice with some ablation support (Table 1).
The progression of style losses from image-level to scene-level to a voxel-based 3D formulation (Eqs. 4-6) is well motivated, and pseudo-code is provided in the appendix.
The two-stage training strategy with a frozen VGGT teacher and color-jitter-as-style trick to avoid trivial identity mapping is sensible.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is largely an assembly of existing components — VGGT backbone, AnySplat-style Gaussian prediction and voxelization, AdaIN/BN-statistics style losses, and a standard cross-attention style-injection scheme. The technical delta over this stack appears modest, and the 'voxel-based 3D style loss' is essentially statistics matching after feature unprojection.

Insufficient evaluation scale: the main SOTA comparison (Tables 3-4) uses only four Tanks and Temples scenes, with no dataset-level aggregation, no variance/statistical significance, and no user study. Conclusions of superiority are drawn from a very small sample.

The closest competing method (Styl3R, an instant stylization approach) is not compared at all; code unavailability is noted but the central claim of state-of-the-art single-forward stylization rests on exactly this comparison. Baselines are limited to two per-scene methods (StyleRF, StyleGS), for which the comparison on consistency metrics is arguably unfair (feed-forward methods inherently produce smoother view consistency).

ArtScore results are questionable: StyleGS scores 0.78 on 'Train' versus 9.50 for Stylos — an extreme outlier that suggests a metric or setup problem, yet it is reported without comment or analysis. StyleRF is missing for Garden entirely.

Claims exceed the evidence: the abstract and contributions claim scaling 'from a single to hundreds of views', but the model is trained on at most 24 views and the paper itself reports visual degradation beyond ~32 views (Fig. 4), including artifacts at 64 views.

Ablation gains are marginal and possibly not meaningful: Table 2 shows 3D style loss improving short-range LPIPS by only 0.000-0.002 over the image loss, and RMSE by ~0.002-0.007, with no uncertainty analysis. The cross-attention ablation (Table 1) uses reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM) as a proxy for stylization quality, which conflates reconstruction fidelity with stylization fidelity.

No evaluation of whether stylization degrades geometry: there is no comparison of reconstruction quality against the underlying base model (AnySplat/VGGT) to support the claim that style conditioning preserves geometric fidelity, which is one of the paper's central claims.

Reproducibility is weak: no code released at submission time, training details (hyperparameters, compute, training duration, view counts) are sparse, and pseudo-code contains vague steps (e.g., 'Resize (C, M, P) to match the resolution' in Algorithm 3) that would be difficult to reproduce exactly.

The paper reports PSNR around 21 dB on CO3D held-out categories without context — there is no baseline indicating whether this reconstruction quality is competitive for feed-forward Gaussian prediction.

Writing issues: duplicated Knapitsch et al. 2017a/b citations, typo in figure captions ('imamge'), the abstract's code link is incomplete, and the first row of Table 1 appears to check both Global and Frame while the text describes three configurations, making the table confusing.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: generalizable, single-forward 3D stylization without per-scene optimization or precomputed poses, which is a meaningful step beyond per-scene 3DGS/NeRF stylization methods.

The design of separating geometry (self-attention backbone path) from style (global cross-attention conditioning) is clearly motivated and directly tested via the frame/global/hybrid ablation (Table 1, Fig. 2).
The voxel-based 3D style loss is a sensible extension of AdaIN-style statistics matching into 3D space, and its progression (image → scene → 3D) is cleanly formulated and ablated (Table 2, Fig. 3).
Evaluation spans category-level (CO3D held-out categories) and cross-scene (DL3DV → Tanks and Temples) generalization, with consistency metrics (short/long-range LPIPS/RMSE) and an artness metric.

Good reproducibility practices: pseudo-code for all three style losses in the appendix, efficiency scaling analysis (time/memory vs. number of views), and a promise to release code and data sources are public.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the geometry backbone, camera/depth heads, and voxelization are directly adopted from VGGT and AnySplat; the core contributions reduce to (i) replacing self-attention with cross-attention for style injection and (ii) computing AdaIN statistics in voxel space—both incremental adaptations of well-known techniques.

Baseline comparison is narrow and potentially misleading: only two baselines (StyleRF, StyleGS) on just four Tanks and Temples scenes, with per-scene methods evaluated on scenes where per-scene fitting is advantageous; no comparison against other generalizable or feed-forward approaches (e.g., RegS, StylizedGS, InstantStyleGaussian), and the most relevant concurrent method Styl3R is deferred to future work. A trivial per-frame 2D stylization baseline is also missing to justify the 3D machinery quantitatively.

Quantitative gains are modest and the evaluation scope is small: Table 2 differences between style losses are marginal (e.g., short-range LPIPS 0.046 vs. 0.048), and the main comparison rests on 4 scenes; no user study supports the 'aesthetically pleasing' claims, and ArtScore is an unvalidated proxy in this context.

Claims exceed the evidence: the paper advertises scaling to 'hundreds of views', yet quality degrades beyond ~32 views and training used at most 24 views; 'zero-shot generalization to unseen categories' is tested on only 3 held-out CO3D categories. The stated geometry–style disentanglement is never quantified with geometry metrics (e.g., depth/pose accuracy under strong styles).

Missing experimental details weaken reproducibility: loss weight hyperparameters (λstyle, λcnt, λclip, λtv, λdistill), training resolution, view sampling strategy, number of Gaussians, and compute budget are not reported; the code-release URL in the abstract is incomplete.

Presentation issues: duplicate citation of Tanks and Temples (2017a/2017b), a typo in Fig. 8/14 captions ('imamge'), and an unexplained result in the ablation (why the hybrid variant, with strictly more information, underperforms the global-only variant).

strengths: Timely and practically significant problem: achieving single-forward, zero-shot 3D stylization without per-scene optimization or precomputed poses addresses a real limitation of existing NeRF/3DGS stylization pipelines, with a striking speed advantage (0.05s vs. minutes for per-scene fitting methods).

Clean architectural design: disentangling geometry (self-attention backbone path) from style (global cross-attention conditioning of color only) is a well-motivated separation, and the ablation (Table 1) provides reasonable evidence that global cross-attention outperforms frame and hybrid coupling.

The voxel-based 3D style loss is a sensible extension of statistics-based style matching into 3D space, and the progressive formulation (image → scene → voxel) makes the contribution easy to follow, with pseudo-code provided.

Extensive evaluation: ablations on style-content coupling, three style loss variants, view-count scaling, plus comparisons against many recent baselines (StyleGaussian, G-Style, StylizedGS, SGSST, Styl3R) using diverse metrics (LPIPS/RMSE consistency, ArtScore, ArtFID, FID, CFSD, etc.), across CO3D, DL3DV, and Tanks & Temples.

Good reproducibility practices: reproducibility statement, released model weights for ablated variants, clarified evaluation protocols in the appendix, and an honest limitations section with categorized failure cases.
Additional useful capabilities demonstrated: multi-style blending and stylization strength control via embedding interpolation, and efficiency/memory scaling analysis.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components are largely assembled from prior work — VGGT backbone (unchanged), CrossBlock from Stytr2, AdaIN-style channel statistics from ArtFlow/Li et al., and voxelization from AnySplat. The voxel 3D style loss is essentially global mean/variance matching after unprojection, a fairly simple extension of existing 2D objectives.

Evidence for the 3D style loss is weak: Table 2 shows near-identical LPIPS (0.047 vs 0.047) and inconsistent RMSE improvements (long-range RMSE ties at 0.142) between scene and 3D losses, with ArtScore differing by only 0.03. The claim that voxel-level matching 'explicitly encodes geometry' and yields 'superior and more stable consistency' is stronger than the numbers support; the ablation is also limited to 15 held-out scenes on one dataset.

Evaluation fairness concerns: single-forward methods are evaluated at reduced resolutions (448/256 px) while per-scene 3DGS baselines use full resolution, which may inflate LPIPS/RMSE consistency scores for Stylos since smoother/blurrier outputs naturally score better. The consistent superiority in consistency metrics could partly reflect resolution and blur rather than genuine 3D consistency.

Inconsistencies in comparison results: on supplementary metrics (Tables 5-6), G-Style frequently outperforms Stylos on FID, LPIPS-gray, and CM loss, and Styl3R achieves better FID on M60/Garden; the abstract-level claims of favorable quality are thus qualified. Styl3R lacks results for the 'Train' scene, and StylizedGS is excluded from headline comparisons due to failure cases, introducing selective reporting.

Contradiction with headline claim: the paper claims scalability 'from a single to hundreds of views,' but admits quality degrades beyond 32 views and that large batches introduce artifacts due to a training gap (max 24 views); scaling to 'hundreds' is not demonstrated.

Missing details weaken reproducibility: the code URL is a placeholder in the main text; the number of Gaussians M, dataset sizes used for the two training stages, and hyperparameter sensitivity are not reported; several Stage-1 design choices (e.g., how reconstruction loss is computed against GT views) are under-specified.

The ArtScore of 4.78 for the image-loss baseline appears anomalous relative to scene (9.12) and 3D (9.15) losses; given that the qualitative differences between scene and 3D losses are subtle, this outlier deserves explanation.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: zero-shot 3D stylization from unposed multi-view images without per-scene optimization, building sensibly on the VGGT/AnySplat line of feed-forward 3D reconstruction.

The paper is clearly written and well organized; the disentanglement of geometry (self-attention path) and style (cross-attention to color embeddings only) is an intuitive design and the two-stage training strategy is described in enough detail to follow.

The progression of style losses (image-level → scene-level → voxel-level, Eq. 3–5) is a clean, well-motivated ablation axis, and the voxel-level 3D style loss is a reasonable extension of statistics-based (AdaIN-style) objectives into 3D space.

The paper is unusually honest in its limitations section (A.5), explicitly cataloguing failure modes and identifying the VGGT backbone as the bottleneck at high view counts, and it provides extensive qualitative results in the appendix.
Efficiency analysis (Fig. 7) of runtime and GPU memory scaling with the number of views is a useful practical contribution.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the architecture is largely an assembly of existing components — VGGT backbone (used unchanged), AnySplat's voxelization, CrossBlock from StyTr2/Deng et al., and AdaIN/Batch-Normalization statistics losses from Li et al. The only genuinely new pieces (the voxel-level style loss and the global cross-attention topology choice) are modest deltas, and the closest contemporaneous work Styl3R already explores feed-forward stylized Gaussian reconstruction.

The claimed benefit of the 3D style loss over the scene-level loss is thin: in Table 2 the 3D loss differs from the scene loss by 0.000 LPIPS (short-range), a 0.003 LPIPS / 0.002 RMSE gain long-range, and 0.03 ArtScore (9.15 vs 9.12). These margins are within plausible noise, yet the paper's central contribution narrative rests on this distinction. No variance estimates, confidence intervals, or additional test scenes are provided.

The evaluation scale is very small: the main comparison (Tables 3–4) uses only four Tanks & Temples scenes, and the core cross-attention ablation (Table 1) uses only three CO3D scenes. Conclusions about generalization to 'unseen categories, scenes, and styles' are not strongly supported by so few test scenes.

Comparison fairness is questionable. Per-scene 3DGS baselines are evaluated on full-resolution images while Stylos is evaluated at 448×448 (and Styl3R at 256×256); perceptual and distributional metrics such as FID, ArtFID, and LPIPS are resolution-sensitive, which may advantage the feed-forward methods in Table 4. This is disclosed only in the appendix.

StylizedGS is excluded from the main quantitative tables because of failure cases on the authors' test styles; while the rationale is explained, selectively dropping a baseline's headline numbers weakens the objectivity of the comparison, and the choice of 'test styles' that cause failures is not justified.

The stylization-time comparison (Table 4) counts training time for per-scene baselines but not training time for Stylos, which required large-scale pretraining on DL3DV-10K plus VGGT initialization; presenting 0.05 s as the cost of stylization overstates the practical advantage.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed: the abstract and Table 3 point to an empty URL ('Our codes are available at .'), and the reproducibility statement says code will be released only 'upon acceptance'. For a paper whose contribution is a system, missing code at review time is a significant limitation.

Several small presentation issues undermine polish: typos ('nearly'→'nearlly', 'varing', 'thruth', 'serveral', 'geomtry'), a missing voxel-size justification (0.002 in what units/scale?), and Eq. 3 indexing a style map as S^l_{b,s} with an unexplained subscript, suggesting the text was not carefully proofread.

The paper does not compare against 2D stylization applied per-view plus the same feed-forward reconstruction, which would isolate how much of the multi-view consistency actually comes from the 3D style loss versus the backbone's inherent multi-view consistency.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: extending feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction (VGGT/AnySplat) with zero-shot, style-conditioned stylization removes per-scene optimization and per-scene fitting, a meaningful step toward practical 3D stylization.

Clean architectural design: separating geometry (self-attention backbone + geometry heads) from appearance (style aggregator with cross-attention + style head) makes the style-geometry disentanglement explicit, and enables nice controllability results (Sec. 4.3 style blending and stylization-strength interpolation).

Comprehensive ablations: the three cross-attention coupling strategies (Table 1) and the progression of style losses from image-level to scene-level to voxel-level (Table 2) directly support the two claimed technical contributions, with qualitative evidence in Figs. 2, 3, 8-10.

Broad comparison against recent 3D stylization methods (StyleGaussian, G-Style, StylizedGS, SGSST, Styl3R) with multiple evaluation axes (consistency, ArtScore/ArtFID, supplementary StyleID-style metrics in Tables 5-6, stylization time), plus an efficiency/memory scaling analysis (A.2).
Good transparency: a limitations section with categorized failure cases (A.5), extensive failure examples (Figs. 11-13), and a reproducibility statement with pseudo-code and planned weight release.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the backbone (VGGT), the Gaussian pipeline and voxelization (AnySplat), the CrossBlock (StyTR2), and the statistics-matching objective (AdaIN/BN statistics, Li et al. 2017) are all existing components; the paper is largely a careful assembly of these with an added voxelized variant of AdaIN. The 3D style loss (Eq. 5, Alg. 1) is conceptually a straightforward extension rather than a fundamentally new objective.

Marginal quantitative gains for the headline contribution: in Table 2 the 3D style loss improves over the scene loss by 0.00-0.02 RMSE, 0.01-0.004 LPIPS, and 0.03 ArtScore (9.15 vs 9.12) - differences that are likely within noise, and no variance/significance analysis is provided. The 'explicitly encodes geometry' claim is mostly supported qualitatively.

Comparison fairness concerns: StylizedGS is dropped from the main quantitative tables due to 'failure cases' on the test styles (A.4), which weakens the completeness of the SOTA comparison; baseline methods are evaluated at full resolution while feed-forward methods use 256x256/448x448, so metrics like ArtFID are not strictly comparable; the ArtFID numbers show G-Style is often clearly better (e.g., 22-26 FID vs 26-29 for Stylos).

Limited evaluation breadth for SOTA comparison: quantitative comparison is on only four Tanks & Temples scenes; ablation metrics are often reported for a handful of scenes ('the pizza scene', 15 held-out scenes), reducing statistical robustness.

Generalization is somewhat overstated: performance degrades notably beyond ~32 views, and the limitations (cluttered scenes, extreme palettes) mean 'zero-shot generalization to unseen categories, scenes, and styles' holds only within a fairly narrow regime; training relies on a color-jittered content view as pseudo-style in Stage 1, whose implications for style diversity are not analyzed.
Code is only promised upon acceptance; the empty link placeholders in the paper limit reproducibility at review time.
